body.objective: Students will be able to develop ideas in a sketchbook.
body.iCan: I can develop ideas in a sketchbook.
successCriteria: I can generate many ideas from a prompt
I can develop one idea through thumbnails and studies
I can reflect on choices in my sketchbook
body.hook: Artists rarely start with a perfect idea. Picasso made dozens of sketches for "Guernica." The sketchbook is where messy ideas get tested, changed and turned into something worth making.

vocabulary.definition: A book for recording ideas, studies and experiments.
The process of generating many ideas.
A small, quick sketch used to test a composition.
The main idea behind an artwork.
A diagram that connects a central idea to related ideas.
Thinking and writing about your choices and what you learned.

study.title: From Prompt to Plan
study.question: How do artists turn a simple prompt into a strong idea?
study.passage:
Prompt: "Something I carry" (an object, a memory, a responsibility or a feeling).
Part 1, Mind map (10 minutes): Write the prompt in the centre of a sketchbook page. Branch out with at least 15 words, objects, places, people and feelings. Circle three that surprise you.
Part 2, Visual research (10 minutes): Collect references: draw two objects from life, take or find two photos, and note one artist who works with a similar idea.
Part 3, Thumbnails (15 minutes): Draw six thumbnails (5 cm by 7 cm) showing different compositions: close-up, bird's-eye view, unusual crop, symbolic object, combined images, empty space.
Part 4, Develop (10 minutes): Choose the strongest thumbnail. Make a larger study testing value or colour.
Part 5, Reflect (5 minutes): Annotate the page: Why this idea? What will you change? What feeling do you want the viewer to have?
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson.
steps: Develop the strongest idea in a study
discussion: Why make six thumbnails instead of one?
Which surprising idea from your mind map led somewhere?
How did visual research change your idea?
What makes a concept personal rather than generic?
study.product: Complete a two-page sketchbook spread (mind map, research, six thumbnails, one developed study, annotations) and a one-paragraph plan for a final artwork.

examples.title: Mind map
examples.problem: Expand "something I carry" with three branches.
examples.answer: Backpack, grandmother's ring, worry about exams

examples.title: Thumbnails
examples.answer: They are quick and force you to think about big shapes and placement, not details
examples.explore: How many could you draw in 10 minutes?

examples.title: Concept
examples.answer: The weight of expectations, shown by an overflowing backpack

examples.title: Annotation
examples.problem: Write a useful annotation for a thumbnail.
examples.answer: "Low viewpoint makes the backpack look huge, like the pressure I feel"

practice.a: A small, quick sketch to test a composition.
The main idea behind an artwork.
A diagram connecting a central idea to related ideas.

practice.q: Why generate many ideas before choosing one?
practice.a: The first idea is often the most obvious; more ideas lead to original ones.

practice.q: Name two kinds of visual research.
practice.a: Drawing from life, photos, artist research.

practice.q: Give two ways to vary a thumbnail composition.
practice.a: Change viewpoint, crop, scale or placement.

practice.q: Why draw from life during research?
practice.a: It builds observation and gives accurate reference.

practice.q: What makes a study different from a thumbnail?
practice.a: A study is larger and tests value, colour or detail.

practice.q: How can a personal concept make art stronger?
practice.a: It gives meaning and originality the viewer can feel.

practice.q: Turn the generic idea "a tree" into a concept.
practice.a: For example, a tree with roots shaped like hands to show family history.

practice.q: Why might an artist abandon an idea in the sketchbook?
practice.a: It doesn't communicate the concept or a better idea emerged.

practice.q: How does reflection improve the next artwork?
practice.a: It identifies what worked and what to change.

misconceptions: Thinking a sketchbook must be neat and finished
Thinking the first idea is the best idea
Thinking research means copying other artists
exitTicket: Draw two quick thumbnails of the same idea from different viewpoints.
Write one annotation explaining a choice.

options: A) learn from choices and plan improvements
items.answer: A) learn from choices and plan improvements

items.q: What is a sketchbook used for?
items.answer: Recording ideas, studies and experiments.

items.q: Define ideation.
items.answer: Generating many ideas.

items.q: Explain why thumbnails are drawn small.
items.answer: To work fast and focus on composition.

items.q: Name three ways to make thumbnails different from each other.
items.answer: Viewpoint, crop, scale, placement or symbolism.

items.q: What is the difference between research and copying?
items.answer: Research gathers references and ideas; copying reproduces another work.

items.q: Write an annotation for a sketch.
items.answer: Answers vary; names a choice and reason.

items.q: Turn a simple subject into a personal concept and explain it.
items.answer: Answers vary.

items.q: Explain how the sketchbook process leads to a stronger final artwork.
items.answer: Testing many ideas and compositions reveals the strongest one and solves problems before the final work.
